name: SSC CHSL
fullName: Staff Selection Commission – Combined Higher Secondary (10+2) Level Examination
approxCandidates: ≈30 lakh+ applicants in recent cycles (approx.; 2026 figure not yet published)
eligibility: Class 12 pass; 18–27 years (with category relaxations); DEO posts in some ministries need Science with Maths at 12th

notification.summary: CHSL 2026 was notified on 7 Sep 2026 for ≈2,536 tentative LDC/JSA, DEO and DEO Grade 'A' vacancies (down from 3,131 in 2025). Applications closed on 7 Oct 2026; an SSC notice dated 1 Oct 2026 schedules the Tier 1 CBT from 30 Nov to 31 Dec 2026 (the earlier calendar had July–September).
notification.source: https://www.careerpower.in/blog/ssc-chsl-exam-date-2026 (secondary report of SSC notice dated 1 Oct 2026; official notices at https://ssc.gov.in)

pattern.notes: Tier 1 is qualifying (shortlisting for Tier 2, where merit is decided). Each section reportedly has its own sectional timer from 2026. Scores are normalised across shifts. 80 minutes for scribe-eligible candidates.

trendAnalysis.summary: CHSL Tier 1 has been easy-to-moderate, slightly easier than CGL Tier 1. Reasoning is the most scoring section (analogy, classification, series, coding, mathematical operations and 4–5 figure-based questions). Quant is arithmetic-heavy (percentage, profit & loss, ratio, average, time-work, speed) with 6–8 questions from algebra, geometry, mensuration and trigonometry and one small DI set. General Awareness is mostly static GK (history, polity, geography, science, culture) with a few current-affairs and sports questions. English is vocabulary and grammar based, with a cloze passage and a short comprehension.

pyqBlueprint.method: Compiled from the commission's published question-paper/response-sheet format and from shift-wise memory-based papers and topic-wise analyses published by coaching sites (Testbook, Adda247, PW, Careers360 day-wise analyses) for the 2023–2025 cycles, cross-checked against the writer's own knowledge of SSC papers. Live web fetches during this round returned only summary pages (SSC barred public discussion of 2025 papers), so question-type detail relies mainly on prior knowledge of the papers; frequencies are approximate per-shift counts. Figure-based (non-verbal) archetypes are recorded but only text-renderable variants are used for generated questions.

archetypes.pattern: Word-pair analogy (A : B :: C : ?) built on a semantic relation – worker : tool, product : raw material, organ : function, instrument : quantity measured, young one : animal; distractors are words of the same category that do not share the relation.

Number-pair/triad analogy where the second term comes from an arithmetic rule on the first (n² ± k, n³ ± k, ×k ± c, digit operations); often framed with two example pairs and a note to operate on whole numbers without splitting digits; distractors satisfy the rule for only one pair or come from ±1 slips.
Letter-cluster analogy (ABCD : EFGH :: ? ) where each letter moves by a fixed or alternating +/− shift or is replaced by its opposite letter (A↔Z); distractors differ in exactly one letter.
Odd-one-out among four words/objects by category or property (three belong to one class, e.g. instruments, organs, rivers of one state); the trap is a surface feature shared by the odd item.
Odd number / number-pair / triad out of four where three follow one arithmetic rule (squares, primes, (a, b, c) with c = a×b − k, divisibility); the odd option breaks the rule by a small margin.
Odd letter-cluster out of four where three clusters have the same positional gaps (e.g. +2, +3 or opposite-letter pairs) and one breaks the gap pattern.
Number series with one missing/next term following a two-step rule (×k + c, alternating operations, differences forming squares/primes or their own series).

Letter or alphanumeric cluster series (e.g. three-letter groups with each position advancing by its own increment, possibly mixed with numbers); find the next cluster; distractors shift one position wrongly.
Word → letter code by a positional rule (each letter shifted by +k/−k, alternate shifts, reversal then shift, or opposite letters); decode the rule from one example and encode a new word.

Word → number code from alphabet positions (sum of positions, sum × k, sum of reverse positions, number of letters × k); apply the rule to a new word; distractors use forward instead of reverse positions.
Sentence coding: two or three short sentences coded as groups of code words; identify the code of a given word by finding the common word/code between statements.
Verbal chain / introduction ('pointing to a photo…') blood relation: trace 3–4 links and name the relation; traps are gender assumptions and the paternal/maternal side.
Coded blood relations: symbols (A + B, A × B, A − B …) stand for relations; decode an expression to find how two people are related, or which expression makes a given relation true.

Walking path of 3–5 legs with left/right turns; find the shortest distance and/or direction from the start (often a Pythagorean triple); or the final facing direction after a sequence of left/right/clockwise turns; traps are direction after a 'right turn' and adding instead of subtracting legs.
Two/three statements ('All/Some/No') with two conclusions; decide which follow, including 'Some … are not' and possibility-type conclusions; trap is reversing 'All A are B'.
Symbol substitution: '+' means '×', '−' means '÷' etc.; rewrite and evaluate an expression with BODMAS; distractors come from left-to-right evaluation.
Which two signs (or two numbers) must be interchanged to make a given equation correct; each option names a pair of signs to swap.
Missing term inside a number sequence (often the middle term) built from a mixed rule such as ×1 + 1, ×2 + 2, ×3 + 3 … or alternating × and +; find the term that replaces '?'.
Defined-operation missing number: from two or three solved examples (a ★ b = …) infer the rule (a² + b², (a + b)², a×b + a …) and apply it; distractors fit just one example.
Number grid / figure (given as rows): each row or column follows the same rule (e.g. third = first × second − k, or sum of squares); find the missing number.

Position from both ends: total in a row/class from two ranks, rank from the other end, persons between two people, or a short comparison chain (taller/older) to find who is at a rank; trap is ±1 counting.
Calendar: day of the week for a date given a reference date (odd-days counting across leap years) or after n days.
Clock angle between the hands at a given time (30H − 5.5M) or time when hands coincide/are opposite.
Overlapping groups described as counts in each region of a three-circle Venn diagram; find how many belong to an exact combination (e.g. both A and B but not C).
Choose the description of the Venn diagram that best represents three classes (one inside another, partial overlap, disjoint).
Mirror image of a clock time or of an alphanumeric/number string (vertical mirror on the right); time question solved by 11:60 − time.
A square sheet is folded once or twice and punched/cut; predict how it looks (number/position of holes) when unfolded.
Count triangles/squares in a figure built from a square or triangle with diagonals and mid-lines.
Figure series / pattern completion: a shape rotates by a fixed angle or gains one element each step; choose the next figure.

Ancient and medieval India: dynasty founders, capitals, rulers' titles, Buddhist/Jain councils, Delhi Sultanate/Mughal/Vijayanagara rulers, battles with years and administrative reforms; distractors are rulers of the same or adjacent dynasty.
Modern India and freedom struggle: founders of organisations/newspapers, INC sessions and presidents, movements with years, Governors-General and their acts.
Article-number question: which Article deals with a given provision (FR, DPSP, office, emergency, finance); distractors are nearby Article numbers.
Constitution-making, Preamble, amendments, schedules and parts with their subject matter (e.g. which Schedule/amendment added X); distractors are adjacent schedules/amendments.
Constitutional/statutory offices: appointment, qualification (age), tenure, removal, oath, and borrowed features of the Constitution.
Indian physical geography: rivers (origin, tributaries, states), lakes, passes, hills, national parks and their states.
Soils, crops, minerals, climate and resources of India (which soil/crop/mineral/region; seasons and winds).
World/physical geography: atmosphere layers, ocean currents, straits, planets, latitudes and landforms.
Banking and monetary policy: RBI instruments (repo, CRR, SLR), functions, institutions and their headquarters.
Economic concepts and planning: GDP/GNP, deficits, inflation measures, Five-Year Plans, taxes, government schemes and their launch.
Physics: SI units and instruments, and everyday phenomena (mirrors/lenses, dispersion, sound speed, heat, electricity).
Chemistry: common names/formulae of compounds, ores and alloys, acids in foods, pH, gases and periodic-table facts.
Human biology: vitamins/minerals and deficiency diseases, organs and glands, blood, diseases and their causative agents.
Plant biology and classification: tissues, photosynthesis, plant hormones, cell organelles, scientists behind classification.
Performing arts and festivals: classical/folk dances, festivals and fairs with their states, instruments and their maestros.
Temples, monuments and architectural styles with their builders/dynasties and locations.
Recent national/international events of the last 1–2 years: summits and hosts, missions, schemes and major appointments.
Sports: number of players, terms and trophies of a sport, venues, and recent Olympic/Asian Games/World Cup results involving India.
Book–author matching (classical and contemporary, including autobiographies) and literary/national award facts.
Unit digit of a power/product or remainder of a large power on division (cyclicity); distractors are adjacent cycle values.
Divisibility and number properties: smallest digit/number to add or subtract for divisibility by 9, 11, 8, which number is divisible, count of factors, primes, or sum of numbers in a range.
BODMAS simplification with fractions/decimals/brackets or 'value of ?' equations; distractors come from wrong operation order.
Basic/successive percentage: x% of a number, net effect of successive increases/decreases, or price rise vs consumption cut.
Percentage word problems: election votes, pass-fail marks, salary spent/saved; find the total or the difference.
Marked price above cost with a discount (or successive discounts) – find profit % or marked price.
Cost/selling price relation: profit % from CP and SP, CP from SP and gain %, CP of x items = SP of y items, two articles sold at the same price, or false-weight dealers.
Simple interest: find rate/time/principal from amounts, or the time to become n times.
Compound interest for 2–3 years, CI − SI difference, or half-yearly compounding.
Divide an amount in a given (sometimes fractional) ratio, or find shares/partnership profit.
Ratio change: number added/subtracted to change a ratio, combined ratio A : B : C, or mean/third proportional.
Average: simple or consecutive-number averages, inclusion/exclusion/replacement of a member (teacher's age, wrong entry corrected), or overlap of first-k and last-k averages.
Two/three workers with individual days; together, one leaves after some days, or efficiency ratio problems.
Pipes and cisterns (filling and emptying pipes together) or men-days (M₁D₁ = M₂D₂) proportionality.
Trains crossing a pole/platform/another train (same or opposite direction) with km/h ↔ m/s conversion.
Average speed for to-and-fro journeys, relative speed/chase problems, or boats and streams.
Reciprocal identities: given x ± 1/x = k, find x² + 1/x², x³ ± 1/x³ or x⁴ + 1/x⁴; distractors from sign slips.
Symmetric identities in a, b, c: (a + b + c)², a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc, or a + b + c = 0 shortcuts; also surds like (√a ± √b).
Triangle properties: angle at incentre/orthocentre, angle-bisector/median length, similarity ratios, Pythagorean right-triangle facts.
Circle theorems: chords intersecting, tangent length, angle in a semicircle, cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles.
Polygons and lines: interior/exterior angles, number of sides or diagonals, angles of a triangle with given ratios.
2-D mensuration: area/perimeter of rectangles, triangles (Heron's), circles and sectors, change in area with change in dimensions.
3-D mensuration: volume/surface area of cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere/hemisphere; melting and recasting.
Standard-angle values and identity simplification (sin²θ + cos²θ, complementary angles like tan 10° tan 80°).
Conditional trigonometry: given sec θ + tan θ, tan θ = a/b or similar, find another ratio/expression.
Small table/bar data (given in text) for 4–6 years or items: ratio, percentage increase, average or difference between categories.
Factual RC question on a 150–250-word passage: answer is stated in the passage; distractors use passage words with altered meaning.
Inference/main-idea/title RC question: choose the central theme or what the author implies.
Vocabulary/tone in context: synonym/antonym of a word used in the passage or the author's tone.
Cloze passage with five numbered blanks; each item tests contextual vocabulary, a connector or a preposition; distractors are near-synonyms that fail the collocation.
Single-sentence blank requiring the contextually correct word (collocation, near-synonym choice).
Single-sentence blank testing grammar – prepositions, articles, tense, conjunctions.
Synonym of a standalone or underlined word (moderate CGL-level vocabulary); distractors include antonyms and look-alike words.
Antonym of a standalone or underlined word; the trap option is a synonym of the given word.
Meaning of a common idiom/phrase (or the idiom that fits a sentence); distractors are literal readings.
One-word substitute for a descriptive phrase (persons, -cide, -phobia, -archy words); distractors are related words of the same family.
Select the correctly (or incorrectly) spelt word among four look-alike spellings (double letters, ie/ei, -ance/-ence).
Sentence split into 3–4 segments; error in subject–verb agreement, pronoun or noun number (each/one of/neither…nor, uncountable nouns).
Sentence split into segments; error in tense sequence, preposition, comparative/superlative, or conjunction pairs (hardly…when, no sooner…than).
Improve the bracketed/underlined part: tense, conditional, preposition or idiom usage; 'No improvement' sometimes an option.
Change active to passive (or vice versa) across tenses, including questions and modals; distractors change the tense.
Direct ↔ indirect speech: reporting verb change, backshift of tense, pronoun and time-word changes; imperatives with 'ordered/requested'.

resources.notes: SSC publishes tentative answer keys with candidates' question papers and response sheets on ssc.gov.in (Answer Key section) for a short window after each Tier; it does not keep a permanent PYQ archive. Memory-based shift papers are compiled by coaching websites.

questions.question:
Select the number that is related to the third number in the same way as the second number is related to the first.
8 : 63 :: 11 : ?

relevance.note: n²−1 number analogy with ±1 distractors; CHSL type though lacks the usual two-pair/NOTE framing

questions.question:
Select the number that will come in place of the question mark (?).
4, 9, 25, 49, 121, ?
questions.explanation: The terms are squares of consecutive prime numbers: 2², 3², 5², 7², 11², so next is 13² = 169.

relevance.note: Squares of consecutive primes series; recurring CHSL series trick

questions.question:
Select the letter that will come next in the series.
B, E, I, N, ?
questions.explanation: Positions 2, 5, 9, 14 (differences +3, +4, +5). Next +6 → 20 = T.

relevance.note: Single-letter series with +3,+4,+5 gaps; CHSL letter-series style

questions.question: In a certain code, ROSE is written as 6821 and CHAIR is written as 73456. How will SEARCH be written in that code?
questions.explanation: From the two words: R = 6, O = 8, S = 2, E = 1, C = 7, H = 3, A = 4, I = 5. SEARCH = S E A R C H = 2 1 4 6 7 3.

relevance.note: Letter-to-digit substitution from two code words; classic CHSL coding

questions.question: Introducing a woman, Arun (a man) said, "She is the wife of the only son of my father." How is the woman related to Arun?
questions.explanation: Arun is a man and the only son of his father is Arun himself. So the woman is Arun's wife.

relevance.note: 'Only son of my father' self-reference trap; frequent CHSL blood relation

questions.question:
If A means '+', B means '−', C means '×' and D means '÷', what is the value of:
18 D 3 C 4 A 6 B 5

relevance.note: Letter-for-sign substitution BODMAS; CHSL format

questions.question:
Select the number that will come in place of the question mark (?).
2, 3, 8, 27, 112, ?

relevance.note: ×n+n series 2,3,8,27,112; exact CHSL missing-term type

questions.question:
Statements:
All roses are flowers.
No flower is a tree.
Conclusions:
I. No rose is a tree.
II. Some trees are roses.
Which conclusion(s) follow(s)?
questions.explanation: All roses lie inside 'flowers', which has no overlap with 'trees', so no rose is a tree (I follows) and II is false.

relevance.note: All-A-B / No-B-C syllogism with conversion trap; CHSL style

questions.question: What is the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock at 4:40?

relevance.note: 30H−5.5M clock angle at 4:40; standard CHSL clock item

questions.question: Who was the first Governor-General of independent India?
questions.explanation: Lord Mountbatten was the first Governor-General of independent India (1947–48); C. Rajagopalachari was the first and only Indian Governor-General.

relevance.note: First Governor-General with Rajagopalachari trap; CHSL modern history

questions.question: Who wrote 'Gita Rahasya' while imprisoned in Mandalay?
questions.explanation: Bal Gangadhar Tilak wrote 'Gita Rahasya' during his imprisonment in Mandalay (1908–1914).

relevance.note: Gita Rahasya–Tilak at Mandalay; typical CHSL book-author history

questions.question: What is the minimum age required to become a member of the Rajya Sabha?
questions.explanation: Article 84 sets the minimum age at 30 years for the Rajya Sabha and 25 years for the Lok Sabha.

relevance.note: Rajya Sabha minimum age with 25/35 traps; CHSL office qualification

questions.question: The Tropic of Cancer does NOT pass through which of the following states?
questions.explanation: The Tropic of Cancer passes through Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram – not Odisha.

relevance.note: Tropic of Cancer state-exclusion question; frequent in CHSL 2023-24

questions.question: Who composed the Sanskrit lyrical poem 'Gita Govinda'?
questions.explanation: 'Gita Govinda' was composed by the 12th-century poet Jayadeva.

relevance.note: Gita Govinda–Jayadeva with other Sanskrit poets as traps; CHSL literature

questions.question: Which of the following numbers is divisible by 11?
questions.explanation: Test: (sum of digits at odd places) − (sum at even places) must be a multiple of 11. 918082: (9 + 8 + 8) − (1 + 0 + 2) = 22 ✓. 918083 gives 25 − 4 = 21, 918092 gives 26 − 3 = 23 and 918081 gives 25 − 2 = 23, none divisible by 11.

relevance.note: Which of four near-identical numbers is divisible by 11; CHSL divisibility

questions.question: What is the value of 36 ÷ 4 × 3 + 15 − 2 × 5?

relevance.note: BODMAS chain with left-to-right ÷×; CHSL simplification

questions.question: The price of sugar rises by 25%. By what percentage must a family reduce its consumption so that its expenditure on sugar does not change?

relevance.note: Price rise 25% → cut 20%; staple CHSL percentage

questions.question: By selling an article for ₹1,170, a man gains 17%. What is its cost price?

relevance.note: CP from SP and gain 17%; CHSL profit

questions.question: Two successive discounts of 20% and 10% are equivalent to a single discount of:

relevance.note: Equivalent of 20% and 10% discounts; CHSL, easy

questions.question: Two numbers are in the ratio 3 : 5. If 9 is subtracted from each, the ratio becomes 12 : 23. What is the smaller number?

relevance.note: Ratio after subtracting 9 → 12:23; CHSL ratio change

questions.question: A man goes from A to B at 40 km/h and returns from B to A at 60 km/h. What is his average speed for the whole journey?
questions.explanation: For equal distances, average speed = 2xy/(x + y) = 2 × 40 × 60/100 = 48 km/h.

relevance.note: Harmonic mean to-and-fro average speed with 50 trap; CHSL

questions.question: If x − 1/x = 4, what is the value of x⁴ + 1/x⁴?

relevance.note: x−1/x → x⁴+1/x⁴ = 322; CHSL algebra with 324 trap

questions.question: Each interior angle of a regular polygon is 140°. How many sides does it have?
questions.explanation: Exterior angle = 180° − 140° = 40°; number of sides = 360°/40° = 9.

relevance.note: Regular polygon sides from interior angle; CHSL geometry

questions.question: What is the value of sin²30° + cos²60° + tan²45°?

relevance.note: Standard-angle sum; CHSL trig

questions.question: A student's marks (out of 100 each): Maths 84, Science 76, English 68, Hindi 72, Social Science 80. By what percentage are his marks in Maths more than his marks in English?

relevance.note: Marks table % more with fractional answer 23 9/17; CHSL DI

questions.question:
Select the one-word substitute for the given phrase.
A person who cannot be corrected or reformed
questions.explanation: Incorrigible = not able to be corrected. Invincible = cannot be defeated; indelible = cannot be erased.

relevance.note: Incorrigible OWS with In- look-alikes; CHSL

questions.question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'necessary' (one 'c', double 's').

relevance.note: Neccessary misspelling; CHSL spelling

questions.question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error, or 'No error'.
One of my friends / have gone to Shimla / for a holiday.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'One' (singular), so 'have gone' should be 'has gone'.

relevance.note: One of my friends have → has; core CHSL agreement error

questions.question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error, or 'No error'.
He gave me / many informations / about the course.
questions.explanation: 'Information' is uncountable; it has no plural. Use 'much information' or 'a lot of information'.

relevance.note: Uncountable 'informations'; CHSL noun error

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate option to improve the bracketed part of the sentence.
He is [senior than me] in service.
questions.explanation: Latin comparatives such as senior, junior, superior and inferior take 'to', not 'than'.

relevance.note: Senior to (Latin comparative); CHSL improvement

questions.question:
Select the passive form of the given sentence.
Who wrote this letter?
options: By whom this letter was written?
Who was this letter written by him?
By whom was this letter written?
By whom has this letter been written?
questions.explanation: Simple past interrogative 'Who wrote …?' becomes 'By whom was … written?' with question word order.

relevance.note: Interrogative passive 'By whom was…'; CHSL

questions.question:
Select the correct indirect form of the given sentence.
He said, "Let us go for a walk."
options: He said that let us go for a walk.
He suggested that we should went for a walk.
He ordered them to go for a walk.
He suggested that they should go for a walk.
questions.explanation: Sentences beginning with 'Let us' (a proposal) are reported with 'suggested/proposed that … should'.

relevance.note: Let us → suggested that they should; CHSL narration

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

The Indian Railways introduced its first passenger train in 1853, running between Bombay and Thane. Since then the network has grown into one of the largest in the world. For millions of people, the railway is not just a means of transport but a lifeline that connects villages to cities, farms to markets and workers to factories. In recent years, the focus has shifted to modernisation: tracks are being electrified, stations redeveloped, and semi-high-speed trains introduced. Critics, however, argue that safety and punctuality deserve as much attention as speed, since a faster train is of little use if it does not arrive on time.

What is the main argument of the critics mentioned in the passage?
options: Safety and punctuality should get as much attention as speed
Electrification of tracks should be stopped
questions.explanation: Critics argue that safety and punctuality deserve as much attention as speed.

relevance.note: Critics' argument RC; CHSL

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

The Indian Railways introduced its first passenger train in 1853, running between Bombay and Thane. Since then the network has grown into one of the largest in the world. For millions of people, the railway is not just a means of transport but a lifeline that connects villages to cities, farms to markets and workers to factories. In recent years, the focus has shifted to modernisation: tracks are being electrified, stations redeveloped, and semi-high-speed trains introduced. Critics, however, argue that safety and punctuality deserve as much attention as speed, since a faster train is of little use if it does not arrive on time.

As used in the passage, 'lifeline' most nearly means:
options: a long rope used in rescues
a line drawn on a railway map
something essential for survival and support
questions.explanation: The railway is described as connecting villages, markets and workers – something people depend on, i.e. essential support.

relevance.note: Contextual meaning 'lifeline' with literal traps; CHSL

questions.question:
Select the option that is related to the third number in the same way as the second number is related to the first number.
(NOTE: Operations should be performed on the whole numbers, without breaking down the numbers into their constituent digits.)
5 : 124 :: 7 : ?

relevance.note: n³−1 with NOTE and 343 trap; exact CHSL format

questions.question:
Select the option that is related to the third letter-cluster in the same way as the second letter-cluster is related to the first letter-cluster.
BDF : HJL :: NPR : ?
questions.explanation: Each letter moves +6: B→H, D→J, F→L. So N→T, P→V, R→X.

relevance.note: +6 shift cluster analogy; CHSL letter analogy

questions.question: Three of the following four letter-clusters are alike in a certain way and one is different. Select the odd letter-cluster.
questions.explanation: BDF, KMO and PRT follow +2, +2. GJL follows +3, +2.

relevance.note: Odd cluster by gap pattern +3+2; CHSL

questions.question: Three of the following four words are alike in a certain way and one is different. Pick the odd one out.
questions.explanation: Sitar, violin and sarod are string instruments; the tabla is a percussion instrument.

relevance.note: Percussion vs string instruments; CHSL classification

questions.question:
Select the letter-cluster that will come next in the following series.
AB, DF, HK, MQ, ?
questions.explanation: First letters: A +3 D +4 H +5 M +6 S. Second letters: B +4 F +5 K +6 Q +7 X. Answer: SX.

relevance.note: Two-letter cluster with growing gaps; CHSL

questions.question: In a certain code language, 'MAT' is coded as 34 and 'SUN' is coded as 54. How will 'CUP' be coded in that language?
questions.explanation: Code = sum of alphabet positions: M13 + A1 + T20 = 34; S19 + U21 + N14 = 54; C3 + U21 + P16 = 40.

relevance.note: Sum-of-positions code with two examples; CHSL

questions.question:
Which two mathematical signs should be interchanged to make the given equation correct?
15 ÷ 6 × 4 + 3 − 5 = 18
questions.explanation: Interchanging ÷ and + gives 15 + 6 × 4 ÷ 3 − 5 = 15 + 8 − 5 = 18. The other swaps give 13.5, −8.4 and 12.

relevance.note: Interchange signs to balance equation; exact CHSL format

questions.question: If 3 @ 4 = 19, 5 @ 2 = 17 and 6 @ 3 = 27, then what is the value of 7 @ 4?

relevance.note: ab+a+b defined operation; CHSL missing number

questions.question: Pointing to a woman, Rohan said, "Her mother is the only daughter of my mother." How is the woman related to Rohan?
questions.explanation: The only daughter of Rohan's mother is Rohan's sister. The woman is his sister's daughter, i.e. his niece.

relevance.note: 'Only daughter of my mother' niece chain; CHSL

questions.question: What is the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock at 3:20?

relevance.note: Clock angle at 3:20; CHSL

questions.question: A wall clock shows the time 4:25. What time will its image show in a plane mirror placed vertically in front of it?

relevance.note: Mirror time 11:60 rule; CHSL mirror clock

questions.question: Which Mughal emperor introduced the Mansabdari system of ranking officials?
questions.explanation: Akbar introduced the Mansabdari system, under which every officer held a rank (mansab).

relevance.note: Mansabdari–Akbar; CHSL medieval history

questions.question: Who founded the 'Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha' in 1924 for the welfare of the depressed classes?
questions.explanation: Dr B. R. Ambedkar founded the Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha in Bombay in 1924.

relevance.note: Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha–Ambedkar; CHSL organisation founder

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India provides for free and compulsory education for all children of the age of six to fourteen years as a Fundamental Right?
questions.explanation: Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Amendment (2002), makes elementary education a Fundamental Right. Article 45 now deals with early childhood care.

relevance.note: Article 21A RTE with Art 45 trap; CHSL article item

questions.question: The Eighth Schedule of the Constitution of India deals with:
options: Allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha
questions.explanation: The Eighth Schedule lists the 22 recognised languages; oaths – Third, Rajya Sabha seats – Fourth, anti-defection – Tenth Schedule.

relevance.note: Eighth Schedule languages with other schedule traps; CHSL

questions.explanation: The Chambal rises in the Vindhyas near Mhow and joins the Yamuna in Uttar Pradesh.

questions.question: A man spends 75% of his monthly income. If his income increases by 20% and his expenditure increases by 10%, by what percentage do his savings increase?

questions.question: Pipe A can fill a tank in 12 hours and pipe B can fill it in 20 hours. If both pipes are opened together, in how many hours will the tank be filled?

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

For centuries, millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi were staple foods across rural India. Hardy and quick to mature, they grow well in dry regions where rice and wheat struggle, and they need far less water and fertiliser. After the Green Revolution, however, high-yielding varieties of rice and wheat were promoted, and millets slowly disappeared from many plates. In recent years nutritionists have drawn attention to their value: millets are rich in fibre, iron and calcium, and they release sugar into the blood slowly. The United Nations declared 2023 the International Year of Millets at India's suggestion, and many state governments now include millets in school meals. Farmers, too, are rediscovering that a crop which survives a weak monsoon is a safer bet in a warming climate.

According to the passage, why did millets disappear from many plates?
options: High-yielding rice and wheat were promoted after the Green Revolution
They needed large amounts of fertiliser
They could not grow in dry regions
The United Nations discouraged their use
questions.explanation: The passage says that after the Green Revolution, high-yielding rice and wheat were promoted and millets slowly disappeared.

relevance.note: Factual RC on millets; CHSL

questions.question:
Read the passage and select the most appropriate option for the numbered blank.

Reading for pleasure is one of the best habits a child can (1) ______. A good story (2) ______ the imagination and teaches new words without any effort. Parents can help by keeping books (3) ______ home and by reading aloud at bedtime. Children who see adults reading are more (4) ______ to pick up a book themselves. Libraries, too, play an important (5) ______ by offering books free of cost.

Select the most appropriate option for blank (3).
questions.explanation: The phrase is 'at home': keeping books at home.

questions.question:
Read the passage and select the most appropriate option for the numbered blank.

Reading for pleasure is one of the best habits a child can (1) ______. A good story (2) ______ the imagination and teaches new words without any effort. Parents can help by keeping books (3) ______ home and by reading aloud at bedtime. Children who see adults reading are more (4) ______ to pick up a book themselves. Libraries, too, play an important (5) ______ by offering books free of cost.

Select the most appropriate option for blank (4).
questions.explanation: 'More likely to + verb' is the correct pattern; 'probable' and 'possible' cannot take a to-infinitive about a person, and 'capable' needs 'of'.

questions.question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A speech delivered without any previous preparation

questions.question: Select the correctly spelt word.

questions.question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error, or 'No error'.
The news about the floods / were shocking / to everyone
questions.explanation: 'News' is an uncountable singular noun, so it takes 'was': 'The news about the floods was shocking.'

questions.question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error, or 'No error'.
She has been living / in Delhi / since five years

I look forward [to meet] you next week.

He was accused ______ theft by his employer.

questions.question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.
He said to me, "What are you doing here?"
options: He asked me what was I doing there.
He asked me what I am doing here.
He asked me what I was doing there.
He told me what I was doing there.
questions.explanation: Questions are reported with 'asked', in statement word order, with the tense backshifted (are doing → was doing) and 'here' changed to 'there'.

relevance.note: Wh-question indirect speech with word-order trap; CHSL

questions.question:
In a certain code language, 'A # B' means 'A is the sister of B', 'A $ B' means 'A is the father of B', 'A % B' means 'A is the wife of B' and 'A & B' means 'A is the son of B'.
If M % N $ P # Q, how is M related to Q?
questions.explanation: M is the wife of N, N is the father of P, and P is the sister of Q. So Q is also N's child and M is Q's mother.

relevance.note: Symbol-coded blood relation with 3 operators, typical CHSL; wife-of-father → mother

questions.question:
Statements:
All pens are markers.
Some markers are erasers.
Conclusions:
I. Some pens are erasers.
II. Some erasers being pens is a possibility.
Which conclusion(s) follow(s)?
questions.explanation: The erasers that are markers need not include any pen, so I does not follow definitely; but such an overlap is possible, so II follows.

relevance.note: All/Some with 'possibility' conclusion is the exact CHSL syllogism trap

questions.question: If 26 January 2026 is a Monday, what day of the week will 2 October 2026 be?
questions.explanation: Days after 26 Jan: 5 (Jan) + 28 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 31 + 30 + 2 = 249 = 35 weeks + 4 days. Monday + 4 = Friday.

relevance.note: Day-of-week from a reference date within a year; odd-day count 249≡4 → Friday, verified

questions.question:
Select the number that will replace the question mark (?) in the following table. The same rule is followed in every row.
Row 1: 5, 3, 34
Row 2: 6, 2, 40
Row 3: 4, 7, ?
questions.explanation: Third number = (first)² + (second)²: 25 + 9 = 34, 36 + 4 = 40, so 16 + 49 = 65.

relevance.note: Row rule a²+b² table; matches CHSL missing-number; 121=(4+7)² is a sound trap

questions.question: Among five friends P, Q, R, S and T, Q is taller than R but shorter than T. P is taller than T but shorter than S. Who is the third tallest?
questions.explanation: Order from tallest: S > P > T > Q > R. The third tallest is T.

relevance.note: Height comparison chain under ranking archetype; CHSL-level, 5 persons, single ordering

questions.question:
Which two mathematical signs should be interchanged to make the given equation correct?
56 ÷ 8 + 6 × 3 − 4 = 1

relevance.note: Exact CHSL sign-interchange format; only ×/− works (7+6−12=1), checked all four

questions.question: In a certain code language, 'BAT' is coded as 58 and 'DOG' is coded as 55. How will 'PEN' be coded in that language?
questions.explanation: Each letter takes its reverse alphabet position (A = 26 … Z = 1): BAT = 25 + 26 + 7 = 58, DOG = 23 + 12 + 20 = 55, PEN = 11 + 22 + 13 = 46. Forward positions give the trap 35.

relevance.note: Reverse-alphabet-position sum code (BAT=58, DOG=55) is a common CHSL numeric coding

questions.question: The 'Iqta' system was institutionalised in the Delhi Sultanate by which ruler?

questions.question: Where is the headquarters of the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD)?

questions.question: Gross National Product (GNP) minus depreciation is equal to:

questions.question: The smell noticed when LPG leaks comes from which compound added to it?

questions.question: Which type of white blood cells is mainly responsible for producing antibodies?

questions.question: What is the compound interest on ₹16,000 for 1 year at 10% per annum, compounded half-yearly?
questions.explanation: Rate 5% per half-year for 2 half-years: CI = 16000 × (1.05² − 1) = 16000 × 0.1025 = ₹1,640. (₹1,600 is the simple interest.)

relevance.note: Half-yearly CI for 1 year; 1600 (SI) and 1680 as realistic slips

questions.question: If a + b + c = 12 and a² + b² + c² = 50, what is the value of ab + bc + ca?
questions.explanation: (a + b + c)² = a² + b² + c² + 2(ab + bc + ca) ⇒ 144 = 50 + 2(ab + bc + ca) ⇒ ab + bc + ca = 47.

relevance.note: (a+b+c)² identity, quick CHSL algebra; 94 (forgot ÷2) is the right trap

questions.question: From an external point P, a tangent PT of length 12 cm is drawn to a circle. A secant through P meets the circle at A and B (A nearer to P) such that PA = 8 cm. What is the length of AB?
questions.explanation: PT² = PA × PB ⇒ 144 = 8 × PB ⇒ PB = 18 cm, so AB = 18 − 8 = 10 cm.

relevance.note: Tangent-secant theorem PT²=PA·PB; 18 (PB) is the classic distractor

questions.question: If sec θ + tan θ = 3, what is the value of sin θ?
questions.explanation: sec θ − tan θ = 1/3. Adding: sec θ = 5/3; subtracting: tan θ = 4/3. sin θ = tan θ / sec θ = 4/5.

relevance.note: sec+tan=k conditional trig exactly as CHSL sets it; 3/5 and 4/3 are swap traps

questions.question: A and B can complete a work in 20 days and 30 days respectively. They start working together, but A leaves 5 days before the work is completed. In how many days is the whole work completed?
questions.explanation: Let the work take T days: (T − 5)/20 + T/30 = 1 ⇒ 3T − 15 + 2T = 60 ⇒ T = 15.

relevance.note: 'A leaves k days before completion' is a standard CHSL time-work twist

questions.question: A train 240 m long, running at 64 km/h, overtakes a man walking at 4 km/h in the same direction. In how much time will it pass him?
questions.explanation: Relative speed = 64 − 4 = 60 km/h = 50/3 m/s. Time = 240 ÷ (50/3) = 14.4 s.

relevance.note: Train overtaking man, same-direction relative speed with km/h→m/s; textbook CHSL

questions.question: The length of a rectangle is increased by 30% and its breadth is decreased by 20%. What is the percentage change in its area?
questions.explanation: New area = 1.3 × 0.8 = 1.04 of the original, i.e. a 4% increase. (30 − 20 = 10% ignores the product term.)

relevance.note: Successive % change in area (x+y+xy/100) is frequent in CHSL mensuration

questions.question:
Read the passage and select the most appropriate option for the numbered blank.

Water is the most precious resource we have, yet we often (1) ______ it as if it would never run out. In many cities, leaking pipes waste a large (2) ______ of treated water every day. Farmers, too, depend heavily (3) ______ groundwater, and wells that were once full are now drying up. Simple measures such as rainwater harvesting and drip irrigation can make a real (4) ______. If each of us is careful, we can (5) ______ that future generations do not face a crisis.

Select the most appropriate option for blank (2).
questions.explanation: Water is uncountable, so 'a large quantity of water' is correct; 'a large number of' needs a countable noun and the idiom is 'a great deal', not 'a large deal'.

relevance.note: Cloze blank: uncountable 'quantity' vs 'number/many' collocation, CHSL style

questions.question:

questions.question:

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
METICULOUS
questions.explanation: Meticulous means showing great attention to detail – painstaking. 'Careless' and 'hasty' are opposites; 'meretricious' is a look-alike meaning showy.

relevance.note: Synonym with lookalike 'Meretricious' and antonyms as traps, typical CHSL vocabulary
